e-7043.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations: Purely Imaginary Eigenvalues
e-7043.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/1ee7ef0a95e618121f4e0653c6beaa64248682ab524ecee8903acec89827e77d.png)
Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/031dd658d772ef4184ceb173311102f64bd0ff3ff5e34321ad4648e0d5026383.png)

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = \textrm{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/d82f994f6426a091fb6fc46b2b2b6fbc66d0b94e7ed1ead3e67257292f4c985b.png)*
e-7043.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/b1ba76ba62019524549b4bcf4c36ec2440b2db8f585150a9456218972363a215.png) 

We are given the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = \textrm{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/f86bdf3e241a51548f8c58fe739e11071197944f5fe2361f83bb34408333211c.png)

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = \overline{\lambda}_1$ is 
$\mathbf{v}_2 = \overline{\mathbf{v}}_1.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = \textrm{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/9b2628d7d3c88303bdd7ed2a8aadcdcfe751a01d910f64972a60cc080d039181.png)

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\text{i}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf w_1$ and $\mathbf w_2$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t) = \cos{t} + \sin{t}.$

Solve the initial value problem
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/4d932848b1d30448dd0135bc75ded935f2065037d4964423899013a47c7a526a.png)
*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = 2\textrm{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/a474b7882cfa32e343d1781a731a4eb540994f72730320d7b8a61639e7e86a14.png)*
e-7044.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/60dd7b0b483c745b0ffda2c89d3216ab463cab5870f91b58b54c7f8e4e446cfd.png)

We are given the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = 2\textrm{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/9e4e860107360ac18ce72e7f4f07dbf9106de041dea3b6c9228cc30bc45c714e.png)

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = \overline{\lambda}_1$ is 
$\mathbf{v}_2 = \overline{\mathbf{v}}_1.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = 2\textrm{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/175d9bde8dda1bfb3a653521add06d23944d72019c0718eed6407abe97f2e87c.png)

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}](\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf w_1$ and $\mathbf w_2$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial condition ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/12f33df5f036901c6069ee03a9ba8ccb05cde1071b7add3d1b310da12bb8298d.png) Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

e-7045.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/471ff0aa856363c49a494f0e711dec8558b429261ddd99685bd0a19416264d05.png) 

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda_1=1+\textrm{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For $\lambda_1 =1+\textrm{i},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/9fbccda402b330b568828c47040f1867c0b075ff434f6d94c2d5d5bcea85f4a8.png)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/91e10c00aed02305fdb5afd421aad57fe52143e3305d84da00819e62f2b30a14.png)

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = \overline{\lambda}_1$ is 
$\mathbf{v}_2 = \overline{\mathbf{v}}_1.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = 1+\textrm{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/2ccc9c4cb7dd95e168690c017e8fca6f92315d1759b3e3ec6bb3a82551b39e3c.png)

We now separate this solution into its real and imaginary parts. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(1+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\text{ } \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf w_1$ and $\mathbf w_2$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t) = \cos{t}.$

So, we get an eigenvector

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = \overline{\lambda}_1$ is 
$\mathbf{v}_2 = \overline{\mathbf{v}}_1.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = 3 + \textrm{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/38fd775722fd8ce56abb0f09499bb0a268ae73b9483a182d4564381557d190cf.png)

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf w_1$ and $\mathbf w_2$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial condition ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068029/assets/f2282999a9f221bd9a14118c116c573f82521e6140d24b008b6fea04c5a61fcf.png) Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}-3[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The imaginary part of (1+2i)e^{2it} is sin(2t)+2cos(2t), so f(t)=sin(2t)+2cos(2t). This also follows from the second equation: 2cos(2t)=f(t)-sin(2t).

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).$

EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[1−51−1].

We are given the eigenvalue λ1=2i and the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1+2i1].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=2i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[1+2i1]e2it.

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain x1(t)=[1+2i1]e2it=[1+2i1]⋅(cos⁡(2t)+isin⁡(2t))=[cos⁡(2t)+isin⁡(2t)+2icos⁡(2t)−2sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)+isin⁡(2t)]=[(cos⁡(2t)−2sin⁡(2t))+i(sin⁡(2t)+2cos⁡(2t))cos⁡(2t)+isin⁡(2t)]=[cos⁡(2t)−2sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)]+i[sin⁡(2t)+2cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)]=w1(t)+iw2(t).

The vectors w1 and w2 are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1w1(t)+c2w2(t)=c1[cos⁡(2t)−2sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)]+c2[sin⁡(2t)+2cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)].

Finally, f(t)=sin⁡(2t)+2cos⁡(2t).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations: Purely Imaginary Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 18 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=12\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=12\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-12\text{i} & 18 \\ -8 & -12\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 3\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{12i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{12i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)-3\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t),\,g(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t).

Find the unknown functions $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}g(t) \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}]

content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 18 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=12\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=12\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-12\text{i} & 18 \\ -8 & -12\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 3\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=12\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{12i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{12i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)-3\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t) \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
f(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t),\,g(t)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(12t).
$$

EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[2−51−2].

We are given the eigenvalue λ1=i and the corresponding eigenvector v1=[2+i1].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[2+i1]eit.

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain x1(t)=[2+i1]eit=[2+i1]⋅(cos⁡t+isin⁡t)=[2cos⁡t+2isin⁡t+icos⁡t−sin⁡tcos⁡t+isin⁡t]=[(2cos⁡t−sin⁡t)+i(cos⁡t+2sin⁡t)cos⁡t+isin⁡t]=[2cos⁡t−sin⁡tcos⁡t]+i[cos⁡t+2sin⁡tsin⁡t]=w1(t)+iw2(t).

content.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\text{i}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$

decision.explanation: Taking the real part of (1-i)e^{3it} gives cos(3t)+sin(3t). Directly, the second equation requires -3sin(3t)=-3f(t)+3cos(3t), confirming f(t)=cos(3t)+sin(3t).

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$

EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−36−33].

We are given the eigenvalue λ1=3i and the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1−i1].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=3i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[1−i1]e3it.

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain x1(t)=[1−i1]e3it=[1−i1]⋅(cos⁡(3t)+isin⁡(3t))=[cos⁡(3t)+isin⁡(3t)−icos⁡(3t)+sin⁡(3t)cos⁡(3t)+isin⁡(3t)]=[(cos⁡(3t)+sin⁡(3t))+i(sin⁡(3t)−cos⁡(3t))cos⁡(3t)+isin⁡(3t)]=[cos⁡(3t)+sin⁡(3t)cos⁡(3t)]+i[sin⁡(3t)−cos⁡(3t)sin⁡(3t)]=w1(t)+iw2(t).

The vectors w1 and w2 are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1w1(t)+c2w2(t)=c1[cos⁡(3t)+sin⁡(3t)cos⁡(3t)]+c2[sin⁡(3t)−cos⁡(3t)sin⁡(3t)].

Finally, f(t)=cos⁡(3t)+sin⁡(3t).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations: Purely Imaginary Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 1 \\ -1 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown functions $f(t)$ and $g(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}g(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}.$*

content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 1 \\ -1 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Question 6
?

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[−126−11]x(t),x(0)=[11].

Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue λ1=5i with the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1−5i1].

a
x(t)=[cos⁡(5t)+sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)]
b
x(t)=[cos⁡(5t)−sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)+sin⁡(5t)]
c
x(t)=[cos⁡(5t)+5sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)]
d
x(t)=[cos⁡(5t)+5sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)−sin⁡(5t)]
e
x(t)=[cos⁡(5t)5sin⁡(4t)+cos⁡(5t)]

decision.explanation: The real part of [1-5i,1]ᵀe^{5it} is [cos(5t)+5sin(5t),cos(5t)]ᵀ, which has initial value [1,1]ᵀ. Its derivative is [25cos(5t)-5sin(5t),-5sin(5t)]ᵀ, equal to A x(t), proving option c.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 26 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 26 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{5\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{5\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-5{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+0[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[−126−11]x(t),x(0)=[11].

Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue λ1=5i with the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1−5i1].

a
x(t)=[cos⁡(5t)+sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)]
b
x(t)=[cos⁡(5t)−sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)+sin⁡(5t)]
c
x(t)=[cos⁡(5t)+5sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)]
d

e

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−126−11].

We are given the eigenvalue λ1=5i and the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1−5i1].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=5i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[1−5i1]e5it.

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain x1(t)=[1−5i1]e5it=[1−5i1]⋅(cos⁡(5t)+isin⁡(5t))=[cos⁡(5t)+isin⁡(5t)−5icos⁡(5t)+5sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)+isin⁡(5t)]=[(cos⁡(5t)+5sin⁡(5t))+i(sin⁡(5t)−5cos⁡(5t))cos⁡(5t)+isin⁡(5t)]=[cos⁡(5t)+5sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)]+i[sin⁡(5t)−5cos⁡(5t)sin⁡(5t)]=w1(t)+iw2(t).

The vectors w1 and w2 are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1w1(t)+c2w2(t)=c1[cos⁡(5t)+5sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)]+c2[sin⁡(5t)−5cos⁡(5t)sin⁡(5t)].

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[11]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=c1[11]+c2[−50][11]=[c1−5c2c1][c1c2]=[10].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=1[cos⁡(5t)+5sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)]+0[sin⁡(5t)−5cos⁡(5t)sin⁡(5t)]=[cos⁡(5t)+5sin⁡(5t)cos⁡(5t)].

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem: Purely Imaginary Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 26 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 26 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{5\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{5\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-5\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Question 7
?

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[−310−13]x(t),x(0)=[1−1].

Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue λ1=i with the corresponding eigenvector v1=[3−i1].

a
x(t)=[cos⁡t−sin⁡t−cos⁡t]
b
x(t)=[cos⁡t−cos⁡t+2sin⁡t]
c
x(t)=[cos⁡t−13sin⁡t−cos⁡t−4sin⁡t]
d
x(t)=[cos⁡t+6sin⁡t−cos⁡t+2sin⁡t]
e
x(t)=[cos⁡t+3sin⁡t−cos⁡t]
Submit

decision.explanation: Since A²=-I, x(t)=x(0)cos(t)+Ax(0)sin(t). Here Ax(0)=[-13,-4]ᵀ, giving x(t)=[cos(t)-13sin(t),-cos(t)-4sin(t)]ᵀ, exactly option c.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 10 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 10 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].$

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}](\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =-[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-13\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[−310−13]x(t),x(0)=[1−1].

Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue λ1=i with the corresponding eigenvector v1=[3−i1].

a
x(t)=[cos⁡t−sin⁡t−cos⁡t]
b
x(t)=[cos⁡t−cos⁡t+2sin⁡t]
c
x(t)=[cos⁡t−13sin⁡t−cos⁡t−4sin⁡t]
d
x(t)=[cos⁡t+6sin⁡t−cos⁡t+2sin⁡t]
e
x(t)=[cos⁡t+3sin⁡t−cos⁡t]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−310−13].

We are given the eigenvalue λ1=i and the corresponding eigenvector v1=[3−i1].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[3−i1]eit.

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain x1(t)=[3−i1]eit=[3−i1](cos⁡t+isin⁡t)=[3cos⁡t+3isin⁡t−icos⁡t+sin⁡tcos⁡t+isin⁡t]=[3cos⁡t+sin⁡t+i(3sin⁡t−cos⁡t)cos⁡t+isin⁡t]=[3cos⁡t+sin⁡tcos⁡t]+i[3sin⁡t−cos⁡tsin⁡t]=w1(t)+iw2(t).

The vectors w1 and w2 are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1w1(t)+c2w2(t)=c1[3cos⁡t+sin⁡tcos⁡t]+c2[3sin⁡t−cos⁡tsin⁡t].

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[1−1]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=c1[31]+c2[−10][1−1]=[3c1−c2c1][c1c2]=[−1−4].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=−[3cos⁡t+sin⁡tcos⁡t]−4[3sin⁡t−cos⁡tsin⁡t]=[cos⁡t−13sin⁡t−cos⁡t−4sin⁡t].

content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 10 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 10 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].$

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}](\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =-[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-13\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since A²=-16I, x(t)=x(0)cos(4t)+(Ax(0)/4)sin(4t). Here Ax(0)=[8,4]ᵀ, so x(t)=[2sin(4t),cos(4t)+sin(4t)]ᵀ, which is option e.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 8 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 8 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−48−44].

We are given the eigenvalue λ1=4i and the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1−i1].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=4i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[1−i1]e4it.

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain x1(t)=[1−i1]e4it=[1−i1]⋅(cos⁡(4t)+isin⁡(4t))=[cos⁡(4t)+isin⁡(4t)−icos⁡(4t)+sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)+isin⁡(4t)]=[(cos⁡(4t)+sin⁡(4t))+i(sin⁡(4t)−cos⁡(4t))cos⁡(4t)+isin⁡(4t)]=[cos⁡(4t)+sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)]+i[sin⁡(4t)−cos⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)]=w1(t)+iw2(t).

The vectors w1 and w2 are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1w1(t)+c2w2(t)=c1[cos⁡(4t)+sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)]+c2[sin⁡(4t)−cos⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)].

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[01]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=c1[11]+c2[−10][01]=[c1−c2c1][c1c2]=[11].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=[cos⁡(4t)+sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)]+[sin⁡(4t)−cos⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)]=[2sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)+sin⁡(4t)].

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem: Purely Imaginary Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 8 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 8 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

?

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[−11−21]x(t),x(0)=[10].

Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue λ1=i with the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1−i2].

a
x(t)=[cos⁡t3sin⁡t]
b
x(t)=[cos⁡t−sin⁡t−2sin⁡t]
c
x(t)=[cos⁡t−sin⁡t]
d
x(t)=[cos⁡t−2sin⁡t−sin⁡t]
e
x(t)=[cos⁡t+sin⁡tsin⁡t]
Submit

decision.explanation: Since A²=-I and Ax(0)=[-1,-2]ᵀ, the solution is x(t)=x(0)cos(t)+Ax(0)sin(t)=[cos(t)-sin(t),-2sin(t)]ᵀ. This satisfies both the differential equation and the initial condition, proving option b.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ 2{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =0[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[−11−21]x(t),x(0)=[10].

Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue λ1=i with the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1−i2].

a
x(t)=[cos⁡t3sin⁡t]
b
x(t)=[cos⁡t−sin⁡t−2sin⁡t]
c
x(t)=[cos⁡t−sin⁡t]
d
x(t)=[cos⁡t−2sin⁡t−sin⁡t]
e
x(t)=[cos⁡t+sin⁡tsin⁡t]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−11−21].

We are given the eigenvalue λ1=i and the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1−i2].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[1−i2]eit.

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain x1(t)=[1−i2]eit=[1−i2]⋅(cos⁡t+isin⁡t)=[cos⁡t+isin⁡t−icos⁡t+sin⁡t2cos⁡t+2isin⁡t]=[(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)+i(sin⁡t−cos⁡t)2cos⁡t+2isin⁡t]=[cos⁡t+sin⁡t2cos⁡t]+i[sin⁡t−cos⁡t2sin⁡t]=w1(t)+iw2(t).

The vectors w1 and w2 are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1w1(t)+c2w2(t)=c1[cos⁡t+sin⁡t2cos⁡t]+c2[sin⁡t−cos⁡t2sin⁡t].

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[10]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=c1[12]+c2[−10][10]=[c1−c22c1][c1c2]=[0−1].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=0[cos⁡t+sin⁡t2cos⁡t]−[sin⁡t−cos⁡t2sin⁡t]=[cos⁡t−sin⁡t−2sin⁡t].

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem: Purely Imaginary Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ 2{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =0[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].$

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}](\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =3[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[−24−22]x(t),x(0)=[03].

Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue λ1=2i with the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1−i1].
