Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−24−22].

We are given the eigenvalue λ1=2i and the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1−i1].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=2i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[1−i1]e2it.

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain x1(t)=[1−i1]e2it=[1−i1](cos⁡(2t)+isin⁡(2t))=[cos⁡(2t)+isin⁡(2t)−icos⁡(2t)+sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)+isin⁡(2t)]=[cos⁡(2t)+sin⁡(2t)+i(sin⁡(2t)−cos⁡(2t))cos⁡(2t)+isin⁡(2t)]=[cos⁡(2t)+sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)]+i[sin⁡(2t)−cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)]=w1(t)+iw2(t).

The vectors w1 and w2 are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1w1(t)+c2w2(t)=c1[cos⁡(2t)+sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)]+c2[sin⁡(2t)−cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)].

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[03]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=c1[11]+c2[−10][03]=[c1−c2c1][c1c2]=[33].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=3[cos⁡(2t)+sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)]+3[sin⁡(2t)−cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)]=[6sin⁡(2t)3cos⁡(2t)+3sin⁡(2t)].

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem: Purely Imaginary Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].$

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2\text{i}t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}](\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\text{i}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\text{i}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =3[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(4+\text{i})t}.

$$

$$

$$

$$

decision.explanation: The second equation is x₂'=x₁+x₂. For the first vector, differentiating e^t cos(2t) gives e^t[cos(2t)-2sin(2t)]. Equating this to e^t[f(t)+cos(2t)] yields f(t)=-2sin(2t), option e.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=1+2\text{i}.$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=1+2\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=1+2\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-2\text{i} & -4 \\ 1 & -2\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+2\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(1+2\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(1+2\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\text{i}(2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).$

after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -15 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4+6\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4+6\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(4+6\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(4+6\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t))+\text{i}{e}^{4t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)) \\ {e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[7−1531].

We are given the eigenvalue λ1=4+6i and the corresponding eigenvector v1=[1+2i1].

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=4+6i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[1+2i1]e(4+6i)t.

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain x1(t)=[1+2i1]e(4+6i)t=[1+2i1]e4t(cos⁡(6t)+isin⁡(6t))=[e4tcos⁡(6t)+ie4tsin⁡(6t)+2ie4tcos⁡(6t)−2e4tsin⁡(6t)e4tcos⁡(6t)+ie4tsin⁡(6t)]=[e4t(cos⁡(6t)−2sin⁡(6t))+ie4t(sin⁡(6t)+2cos⁡(6t))e4tcos⁡(6t)+ie4tsin⁡(6t)]=[cos⁡(6t)−2sin⁡(6t)cos⁡(6t)]e4t+i[sin⁡(6t)+2cos⁡(6t)sin⁡(6t)]e4t=w1(t)+iw2(t).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations: Complex Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}7 & -15 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4+6\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -15 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4+6\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4+6\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(4+6\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(4+6\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t))+\text{i}{e}^{4t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)) \\ {e}^{4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}{e}^{4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t).$

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}7 & -10 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6+3\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -10 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6+3\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6+3\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(6+3\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(6+3\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}{e}^{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\text{i}{e}^{6t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3{e}^{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {e}^{6t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}{e}^{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+\text{i}{e}^{6t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ {e}^{6t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}{e}^{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations: Complex Eigenvalues
content.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}7 & -10 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6+3\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -10 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6+3\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6+3\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(6+3\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(6+3\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}{e}^{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\text{i}{e}^{6t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3{e}^{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {e}^{6t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}{e}^{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+\text{i}{e}^{6t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ {e}^{6t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}{e}^{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$

before.name: Question 15
before.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above.
Find the unknown function $f(t)$ in the general solution to the system, shown below.

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=1+2\text{i}.$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=1+2\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=1+2\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-2\text{i} & -2 \\ 2 & -2\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+2\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(1+2\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(1+2\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\text{i}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).$

\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(1+2\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\text{i}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).$

Question 16
?

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[15−15]x(t),x(0)=[1−1].

Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue λ1=3+i with the corresponding eigenvector v1=[2−i1].

a
x(t)=[cos⁡t+25sin⁡t−cos⁡t]e3t
b
x(t)=[cos⁡t+2sin⁡t−cos⁡t−7sin⁡t]e3t
c
x(t)=[cos⁡t−7sin⁡t−cos⁡t−3sin⁡t]e3t
d
x(t)=[cos⁡t−cos⁡t−5sin⁡t]e3t
e
x(t)=[cos⁡t−cos⁡t]e3t
Submit

decision.explanation: Let B=A-3I. Then B²=-I and Bx(0)=[-7,-3]ᵀ. Therefore x(t)=e^{3t}[x(0)cos(t)+Bx(0)sin(t)]=e^{3t}[cos(t)-7sin(t),-cos(t)-3sin(t)]ᵀ, proving option c.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =-[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}-3[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16
?

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[15−15]x(t),x(0)=[1−1].

Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue λ1=3+i with the corresponding eigenvector v1=[2−i1].

a
x(t)=[cos⁡t+25sin⁡t−cos⁡t]e3t
b

x(t)=[cos⁡t−cos⁡t−5sin⁡t]e3t
e
x(t)=[cos⁡t−cos⁡t]e3t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[15−15].

We are given the eigenvalue λ1=3+i and the corresponding eigenvector v1=[2−i1].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=3+i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[2−i1]e(3+i)t. We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

x1(t)=[2−i1]e(3+i)t=[2−i1]e3t(cos⁡t+isin⁡t)=[2e3tcos⁡t+2ie3tsin⁡t−ie3tcos⁡t+e3tsin⁡te3tcos⁡t+ie3tsin⁡t]=[2cos⁡t+sin⁡tcos⁡t]e3t+i[2sin⁡t−cos⁡tsin⁡t]e3t=w1(t)+iw2(t).

The vectors w1 and w2 are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1w1(t)+c2w2(t)=c1[2cos⁡t+sin⁡tcos⁡t]e3t+c2[2sin⁡t−cos⁡tsin⁡t]e3t.

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[1−1]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=c1[21]+c2[−10][1−1]=[2c1−c2c1][c1c2]=[−1−3].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=−[2cos⁡t+sin⁡tcos⁡t]e3t−3[2sin⁡t−cos⁡tsin⁡t]e3t=[cos⁡t−7sin⁡t−cos⁡t−3sin⁡t]e3t.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem: Complex Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(3+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\text{i}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =-[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}-3[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is λ1=−2+i.

a

b

c

e

decision.explanation: Let B=A+2I. Then B²=-I and Bx(0)=[-2,-1]ᵀ. Hence x(t)=e^{-2t}[x(0)cos(t)+Bx(0)sin(t)]=e^{-2t}[-cos(t)-2sin(t),2cos(t)-sin(t)]ᵀ, which is option a.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+\text{i}.$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & -1 \\ 1 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-2+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-2+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i}{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =2[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}-[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is λ1=−2+i.

EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−2−11−2].

We are given that the eigenvalue is λ1=−2+i.

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For λ1=−2+i, we get A−λ1I=[−i−11−i]∼[1−i00]. So, we get an eigenvector v1=[i1].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=−2+i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[i1]e(−2+i)t. We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

x1(t)=[i1]e(−2+i)t=[i1]e−2t(cos⁡t+isin⁡t)=[ie−2tcos⁡t−e−2tsin⁡te−2tcos⁡t+ie−2tsin⁡t]=[−sin⁡tcos⁡t]e−2t+i[cos⁡tsin⁡t]e−2t=w1(t)+iw2(t).

The vectors w1 and w2 are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1w1(t)+c2w2(t)=c1[−sin⁡tcos⁡t]e−2t+c2[cos⁡tsin⁡t]e−2t.

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[−12]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=c1[01]+c2[10][−12]=[c2c1].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=2[−sin⁡tcos⁡t]e−2t−[cos⁡tsin⁡t]e−2t=[−cos⁡t−2sin⁡t2cos⁡t−sin⁡t]e−2t.

This yields the displayed option a and satisfies the initial condition and differential equation. The deliberately submitted option c is incorrect.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem: Complex Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+\text{i}.$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & -1 \\ 1 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-2+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-2+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i}{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{-2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{-2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =2[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}-[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 18
after.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3+2\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3+2\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3+2\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-3+2\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-3+2\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\text{i}{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\text{i}{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {e}^{-3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+\text{i}{e}^{-3t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ {e}^{-3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =2[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}-3[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-10\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem: Complex Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3+2\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3+2\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3+2\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-3+2\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(-3+2\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\text{i}{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\text{i}{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {e}^{-3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+\text{i}{e}^{-3t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ {e}^{-3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}{e}^{-3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =2[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}-3[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-10\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

Solve the initial value problem x′(t)=[5−101−1]x(t),x(0)=[−6−2].

Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue λ1=2+i with the corresponding eigenvector v1=[3+i1].

a
x(t)=[−6cos⁡t−5sin⁡t−2cos⁡t]e2t
b
x(t)=[3sin⁡t−6cos⁡t2sin⁡t−2cos⁡t]e2t
c
x(t)=[2sin⁡t−6cos⁡t−2cos⁡t]e2t
d
x(t)=[−sin⁡t−6cos⁡t−2cos⁡t]e2t
e
x(t)=[−6cos⁡t10sin⁡t−2cos⁡t]e2t
Submit

decision.explanation: Let B=A-2I. Then B²=-I and Bx(0)=[2,0]ᵀ. Therefore x(t)=e^{2t}[x(0)cos(t)+Bx(0)sin(t)]=e^{2t}[2sin(t)-6cos(t),-2cos(t)]ᵀ, proving option c.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(2+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(2+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}(3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\text{i}({e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}(3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =-2[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+0[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-6\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[5−101−1].

We are given the eigenvalue λ1=2+i and the corresponding eigenvector v1=[3+i1].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=2+i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[3+i1]e(2+i)t. We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

x1(t)=[3+i1]e(2+i)t=[3+i1]e2t(cos⁡t+isin⁡t)=[3e2tcos⁡t+i(3e2tsin⁡t)+i(e2tcos⁡t)−e2tsin⁡te2tcos⁡t+i(e2tsin⁡t)]=[3e2tcos⁡t−e2tsin⁡t+i(3e2tsin⁡t+e2tcos⁡t)e2tcos⁡t+i(e2tsin⁡t)]=[3cos⁡t−sin⁡tcos⁡t]e2t+i[3sin⁡t+cos⁡tsin⁡t]e2t=w1(t)+iw2(t).

The vectors w1 and w2 are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1w1(t)+c2w2(t)=c1[3cos⁡t−sin⁡tcos⁡t]e2t+c2[3sin⁡t+cos⁡tsin⁡t]e2t.

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[−6−2]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=c1[31]+c2[10][−6−2]=[3c1+c2c1][c1c2]=[−20].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=−2[3cos⁡t−sin⁡tcos⁡t]e2t+0[3sin⁡t+cos⁡tsin⁡t]e2t=[2sin⁡t−6cos⁡t−2cos⁡t]e2t.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem: Complex Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(2+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(2+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}(3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\text{i}({e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}(3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =-2[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+0[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-6\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(2+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(2+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3+\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}(3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\text{i}({e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}(3{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}({e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$

$$

decision.explanation: For option b, x(0)=[0,1]ᵀ. Differentiating gives x'(t)=e^t[sin(t)+cos(t),cos(t)-sin(t)]ᵀ, which equals Ax(t). Thus option b satisfies the initial value problem.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=1+\text{i}.$*
after.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=1+\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=1+\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 1 \\ -1 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(1+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(1+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i}{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+0[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is λ1=1+i.

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix A=[11−11].

We are given that the eigenvalue is λ1=1+i.

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For λ1=1+i, we get A−λ1I=[−i1−1−i]∼[1i00]. So, we get an eigenvector v1=[−i1].

Note: The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue λ2=λ―1 is v2=v―1. But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue λ1=1+i and its associated eigenvector is x1(t)=[−i1]e(1+i)t.

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain x1(t)=[−i1]e(1+i)t=[−i1]et(cos⁡t+isin⁡t)=[−ietcos⁡t+etsin⁡tetcos⁡t+ietsin⁡t]=[sin⁡tcos⁡t]et+i[−cos⁡tsin⁡t]et=w1(t)+iw2(t).

The vectors w1 and w2 are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is x(t)=c1w1(t)+c2w2(t)=c1[sin⁡tcos⁡t]et+c2[−cos⁡tsin⁡t]et.

Now, we need to find the values of c1 and c2 using the initial condition x(0)=[01]. Substituting t=0 into the general solution gives x(0)=c1[01]+c2[−10][01]=[−c2c1][c1c2]=[10].

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by x(t)=1[sin⁡tcos⁡t]et+0[−cos⁡tsin⁡t]et=[sin⁡tcos⁡t]et.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem: Complex Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

*Hint: One of the eigenvalues of the matrix is ${\lambda }_{1}=1+\text{i}.$*
content.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

We are given that the eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=1+\text{i}.$ 

Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors. For ${\lambda }_{1}=1+\text{i},$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 1 \\ -1 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & \text{i} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(1+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{(1+\text{i})t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i}{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\text{i}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+0[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$
